bodyText:
What is an Operating System?

An operating system (OS) is system software that acts as an intermediary between the user and the computer hardware. It manages all hardware and software resources and provides an environment in which the user can execute programs conveniently and efficiently. Without an operating system, a user would have to manage the processor, memory, input and output devices, and files directly.

The kernel is the core part of the operating system. It is the program that runs at all times in the computer, while other programs are applications. The shell is the interface between the user and the kernel; it interprets user commands and passes them to the kernel.

Main Functions of an Operating System

  • Process management: creating, scheduling, suspending, resuming and terminating processes, and handling inter-process communication and synchronisation.
  • Memory management: allocating and deallocating memory, keeping track of which parts of memory are in use, and deciding which processes to load when memory becomes available.
  • File management: creating, organising, storing, retrieving and protecting files and directories on storage devices.
  • Device management: controlling input and output devices through device drivers, handling interrupts, and allocating devices to processes.
  • Security and protection: authenticating users, controlling access to resources, and protecting data from unauthorised access and malware.
  • User interface: providing a command-line interface (CLI), graphical user interface (GUI), or both, through which users interact with the computer.
  • Error detection and handling: monitoring the system for errors in hardware and software and taking corrective action.
  • Resource allocation and accounting: fairly distributing processor time, memory and devices among competing programs, and keeping records of resource use.

Types of Operating Systems

Batch operating systems group similar jobs together and execute them without user interaction. This improves processor utilisation but gives no interaction while a job runs. Time-sharing (multiprogramming) systems allow several users to share the processor at the same time by switching rapidly between jobs, giving each user the impression of a dedicated machine.

Multiprocessing systems use two or more processors in a single computer, sharing memory and the operating system. Distributed operating systems manage a collection of independent computers that appear to users as a single coherent system. Real-time operating systems (RTOS) must respond to inputs within a strict time limit; hard real-time systems guarantee deadlines, while soft real-time systems try to meet them but may occasionally miss one.

Other important types include single-user and multi-user systems, network operating systems that provide services over a network, and embedded operating systems built into devices such as washing machines and traffic controllers.

History and Examples for Exams

The GM-NAA I/O system, developed in 1956 for the IBM 704, is generally regarded as the first operating system. UNIX was developed at Bell Labs in 1969 by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie and was written largely in the C language. MS-DOS was released in 1981, Microsoft Windows 1.0 in 1985, and the Linux kernel was first released by Linus Torvalds in 1991. Android, based on the Linux kernel, is the most widely used mobile operating system, while iOS is used on Apple mobile devices and macOS on Apple computers.

bodyText:
Process and Program

A program is a passive entity stored on disk, whereas a process is a program in execution. A process includes the program code, its current activity (program counter and processor registers), its stack, its data section, and its heap. Two processes may run the same program, but each has its own separate memory and state.

A process passes through several states during its life. In the new state it is being created; in the ready state it is waiting to be assigned to a processor; in the running state instructions are being executed; in the waiting state it is waiting for an event such as input or output completion; and in the terminated state it has finished execution. The process control block (PCB) stores all information about a process, including its state, program counter, processor registers, scheduling information, memory limits, and list of open files.

Context Switch and Threads

A context switch occurs when the processor switches from one process to another. The operating system saves the state of the old process in its PCB and loads the saved state of the new process. A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process; threads of the same process share code, data and open files but have their own registers and stack. Multithreading improves responsiveness and resource sharing but requires careful synchronisation.

CPU Scheduling

CPU scheduling selects which ready process runs next on the processor. Its goals include maximum processor utilisation, maximum throughput (number of processes completed per unit time), minimum turnaround time (time from submission to completion), minimum waiting time (time spent in the ready queue), and minimum response time (time from submission to first response).

First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) schedules processes in arrival order; it is simple but can cause the convoy effect, where short processes wait behind one long process. Shortest-Job-First (SJF) schedules the process with the smallest next CPU burst and gives the minimum average waiting time, but the length of the next burst cannot be known exactly in practice. Round Robin (RR) gives each process a fixed time quantum in turn; a short quantum improves response time but increases context-switch overhead. Priority scheduling assigns a priority to each process and runs the highest priority first; it can cause starvation of low-priority processes, which is handled by aging, gradually increasing the priority of waiting processes. Multilevel queue scheduling divides the ready queue into separate queues, for example foreground and background queues, each with its own scheduling algorithm.
keyPoints: A program is a passive entity on disk, while a process is a program in execution.
The five basic process states are New, Ready, Running, Waiting and Terminated.

A context switch is the saving of one process state and loading of another when the processor changes processes.
A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process; threads of one process share code and data but have separate registers and stacks.
Throughput is the number of processes completed per unit of time.
Turnaround time is the total time from submission of a process to its completion.

The convoy effect is when short processes wait behind one long process under FCFS scheduling.

Starvation is when a low-priority process waits indefinitely; aging gradually raises the priority of waiting processes to prevent it.

bodyText:
Why Memory Management is Needed

Memory management allocates main memory to processes, keeps track of which parts are free and which are in use, and protects one process memory from another. The main goals are efficient utilisation of memory, protection, sharing, and allowing a logical address space larger than physical memory through virtual memory.

Logical addresses are generated by the processor and used by a program, while physical addresses are the actual locations in main memory. The memory management unit (MMU) maps logical addresses to physical addresses at run time. In contiguous allocation, each process occupies a single continuous block of memory; this is simple but suffers from fragmentation.

Fragmentation

External fragmentation occurs when free memory exists in total but not in one continuous block large enough for a process, so the process cannot be loaded despite enough total free space. Internal fragmentation occurs when a fixed-size block allocated to a process is larger than the process needs, so memory inside the block is wasted. Compaction, gathering scattered free blocks into one large block, can reduce external fragmentation but is costly.

Paging

Paging divides physical memory into fixed-size blocks called frames and divides a process logical memory into blocks of the same size called pages. A page table maps each page to the frame where it is stored, so a process need not occupy contiguous memory. Paging eliminates external fragmentation, although the last page of a process may suffer internal fragmentation. The page size is a power of two, commonly 4 KB on modern systems.

Segmentation

Segmentation divides a process logical memory into variable-size segments that reflect the logical structure of the program, such as code, data, stack and functions. Each segment has a name, a length and a base address, and the segment table maps segment numbers to their base addresses and limits. Segmentation matches the programmer view of memory and allows segments to grow independently, but it can suffer from external fragmentation because segments are variable in size.

Virtual Memory and Page Replacement

Virtual memory allows a process to execute even when it is not fully loaded in main memory, using demand paging: pages are loaded only when they are needed. When a needed page is absent, a page fault occurs and the operating system loads the page from disk. If memory is full, a page replacement algorithm chooses a victim page to remove. First-In, First-Out (FIFO) removes the oldest page; Least Recently Used (LRU) removes the page unused for the longest time and is a good approximation of the optimal algorithm; the optimal algorithm removes the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future, but it cannot be implemented in practice because future references are unknown.

bodyText:
Files and File Systems

A file is a collection of related information stored on secondary storage, such as a disk. A file system is the method an operating system uses to organise, store, retrieve and manage files on a storage device. It defines how file names, directories, metadata, access permissions and free space are handled, and how the operating system locates data on disk.

A directory is a structure that organises files, often in a tree hierarchy with a root directory at the top. File attributes (metadata) include the file name, type, location, size, owner, creation and modification times, and access permissions. Common file operations are creating, opening, reading, writing, renaming, deleting and closing a file.

FAT File System

FAT stands for File Allocation Table. It was introduced by Microsoft for MS-DOS and early Windows systems. The File Allocation Table is a table at the start of the volume that records which clusters are used by each file and which are free, forming a linked chain for each file. FAT12, FAT16 and FAT32 are versions named for the number of bits used for cluster addresses. FAT32, introduced with Windows 95 OSR2 in 1996, supports larger volumes than FAT16 but has a maximum single-file size of 4 GB, and it has no built-in file permissions or journaling.

NTFS File System

NTFS stands for New Technology File System. It was introduced by Microsoft with Windows NT in 1993 and became the standard file system for Windows. NTFS supports large files and volumes, file-level security and permissions, encryption through the Encrypting File System (EFS), compression, disk quotas, and journaling, which records changes before they are written so the file system can recover more reliably after a crash. NTFS uses a Master File Table (MFT) to store metadata for every file and directory.

ext File Systems

The ext family is the standard file system family for Linux. ext2, introduced in 1993, was the first widely used Linux file system but had no journaling. ext3, introduced in 2001, added journaling to ext2. ext4, introduced in 2008 and now the default on many Linux distributions, supports larger files and volumes than ext3, uses extents (groups of contiguous blocks) instead of individual block pointers for efficiency, supports delayed allocation, and retains journaling. Unlike FAT, ext file systems use inodes: each file has an inode storing its metadata and pointers to its data blocks.

Journaling

Journaling means writing a log (journal) of intended changes before applying them to the file system. If the system crashes mid-write, the journal allows the file system to replay or roll back incomplete changes, greatly reducing the risk of corruption. NTFS, ext3 and ext4 are journaling file systems; FAT is not.

bodyText:
What is a Deadlock?

A deadlock is a situation in which a set of processes are blocked because each process is holding a resource and waiting for a resource held by another process in the set, so none of them can ever proceed. The classic example is two processes and two resources: Process A holds Resource 1 and waits for Resource 2, while Process B holds Resource 2 and waits for Resource 1. Neither can continue.

Deadlock is different from starvation. In deadlock, no process in the set can proceed at all. In starvation, a process waits indefinitely because other processes keep being given priority, but the system as a whole continues to make progress.

The Four Necessary Conditions (Coffman Conditions)

Deadlock can occur only if all four of the following conditions hold at the same time. If any one of them is absent, deadlock cannot occur. They were described by Edward G. Coffman Jr. and colleagues in 1971.

  • Mutual exclusion: at least one resource is held in a non-shareable mode, so only one process can use it at a time.
  • Hold and wait: a process holds at least one resource while waiting to acquire additional resources held by other processes.
  • No preemption: a resource can be released only voluntarily by the process holding it, after it has completed its task; it cannot be forcibly taken away.
  • Circular wait: a set of processes exists such that each process waits for a resource held by the next process in the set, forming a cycle.

Handling Deadlocks

There are four main strategies for dealing with deadlocks. Deadlock prevention breaks at least one of the four necessary conditions, for example by requiring a process to request all its resources at once (breaking hold and wait) or by imposing an ordering on resources so circular wait cannot form. Deadlock avoidance uses advance information about maximum resource needs, with the Banker algorithm (proposed by Edsger Dijkstra) granting a request only if the resulting state is a safe state, meaning all processes can still finish.

Deadlock detection and recovery allows deadlocks to happen, periodically checks for them using a wait-for graph or resource-allocation graph, and then recovers by aborting one or more processes in the cycle or by preempting resources from a process and rolling it back. The fourth strategy is to ignore the problem entirely, on the grounds that deadlocks are rare and prevention or avoidance costs more than an occasional manual restart; this is the approach taken by most operating systems, including UNIX and Windows, and it is sometimes called the ostrich algorithm.

Resource-Allocation Graph

A resource-allocation graph shows processes as circles and resources as squares, with a request edge from a process to a resource and an assignment edge from a resource to a process. A cycle in the graph indicates that deadlock may exist; if each resource has only one instance, a cycle proves deadlock, while with multiple instances a cycle is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock.
keyPoints: Deadlock is a situation where a set of processes are blocked, each holding a resource and waiting for one held by another in the set.
Deadlock differs from starvation: in deadlock no process in the set can proceed, while in starvation the system as a whole still progresses.
The four necessary Coffman conditions for deadlock are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait.
The Coffman conditions were described by Edward G. Coffman Jr. and colleagues in 1971.

Hold and wait means a process holds one resource while waiting for additional resources held by others.

Circular wait means processes form a cycle, each waiting for a resource held by the next process in the cycle.
Deadlock prevention works by breaking at least one of the four necessary conditions.
The Banker algorithm, proposed by Edsger Dijkstra, is used for deadlock avoidance and grants a request only if the resulting state is safe.
A safe state is one in which all processes can still complete their execution.
The ostrich algorithm means ignoring deadlocks entirely; it is the approach taken by most operating systems, including UNIX and Windows.
